header.title: Homiliae [Sp.]: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Clemens Romanus (Clement of Rome)
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg1271.tlg006.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1271.tlg006.1st1K-gr: The opening sentence is loosely built in the Greek (φάσκων ... λέγει, 'claiming ... he says'), and in the account of the making it is not always clear whether the subject is Simon or the spirit.
ἀφοβίας αἰτίαν (8.12), 'as a cause of fearlessness', is obscure; it seems to mean that the poets' tales embolden wrongdoers.
ἰδίου τινὸς γένους (8.18), 'some kind of their own', may refer to food proper to them. θνητοῦ (8.19), literally 'mortal', is taken as an animal that has died of itself.

nodes.text: For he even began to commit murder, as he himself, still as a friend to friends, disclosed: that, having separated the soul of a child from its own body by unspeakable oaths, [to be his] helper in making appear whatever he pleases, and having painted the boy's portrait, he keeps it set up in the inner room where he himself sleeps; claiming that he once formed this [boy] out of air by divine transformations and, having painted his form, he says he gave him back again to the air. And he explains that he did the deed in this way. First, he says, the human spirit, turned into the nature of heat, drew in and swallowed the surrounding air like a cupping-glass; then, when it had come inside the form of the spirit, he turned it into water; and since it could not flow away because of the cohesion of the spirit, he said he changed the air in it into the nature of blood, and the blood, congealing, made flesh; and then, the flesh having thus solidified, he produced a man not from earth but from air. And having thus persuaded himself that he could make a new man, he said he had undone the transformations and given him back again to the air. And when he told these things to others he was believed, but by us, who were present with him at the rite, he was, in piety, disbelieved. Therefore, condemning [him] for impiety, we left him.

When Aquila had said this, I, Clement, asked what, then, are the marvels he does. And they told me that he makes statues walk, and rolls on fire and is not burned; sometimes he even flies; and he makes loaves from stones; he becomes a serpent, is transformed into a goat, becomes two-faced, changes into gold; he opens locked doors, melts iron, at dinners he presents phantoms of all kinds of shapes; he makes the vessels in a house be seen moving as if of their own accord to serve, while those who carry them are not seen. As I listened to them saying these things I was amazed. And many testified that they had themselves been present and witnessed such things.

Having foreseen this about Apion, as soon as he asked the cause of my illness, I answered, pretending, that I was suffering what the young suffer and was sick at heart. And he said to this: Child, speak boldly, as to a father: what is the sickness of your soul? And when I again sighed, pretending, as though ashamed to speak about love, by my silence and by looking down I gave him the suspicion of what I wanted to convey. And he, truly convinced that I was in love with a woman, said: There is nothing in life for which help cannot be had. For I myself too, when I was young, fell in love with a most distinguished woman, and not only thought it impossible to win her, but did not even hope ever to speak to her; and yet, meeting a certain Egyptian, a thorough master of the magicians' arts, and becoming his friend, I disclosed my love to him; and not only did he put himself at my service for everything I wanted, but, showing me still more generous goodwill, he did not begrudge teaching me the incantation too, by which I won her. And by his secret instruction, trusting the generosity of the one who taught me, and succeeding once, I ceased to be in love.

For of the spirits who dwell in heaven, the angels who inhabit the lowest region, vexed at the ingratitude of men towards God, ask to come into the life of men, so that, by truly becoming men and by a superior way of life, they might convict those who had been ungrateful to him and there subject each to the punishment he deserved. When, then, they had asked and received [this], they changed themselves into every kind of nature, since they were of a more divine substance and could easily be transformed into anything. And they became precious stone, and splendid pearl, and purple of the most beautiful kind, and glorious gold, and every very costly material. And they fell into the hands of some and into the laps of others, and willingly let themselves be stolen by them. They also changed into four-footed beasts and reptiles, swimming and flying creatures, and into whatever they wished. These things your poets too sing of, at random, as a cause of fearlessness, assigning to one [being] the many and various deeds of all.

But when, having become these things, they had convicted the greedy who seized them, and had changed themselves into human nature, so that, by living holily and showing that it is possible to live [so], they might bring the ungrateful to account, then, since they had in every respect truly become men and had human desire, overcome by it they slipped into intercourse with women; and having been entangled with them, and set fast in defilement, and wholly emptied of their first power, they were unable to change the limbs that had been turned from fire back into the original purity of their own nature. For because of the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh, they travelled the impious road downward; for they themselves, fettered with the bonds of flesh, are held fast and strongly bound, and for this reason they were no longer able to go up into the heavens.

For after intercourse, when they were asked for what they had at first become and could no longer supply it, because after their defilement they could not make themselves into anything else, and wishing to please the women they loved, they showed them, instead of themselves, the marrow of the earth, I mean the flowers of the mines: gold, bronze, silver, iron and the like, together with all the most precious stones. And along with these enchanted stones they also handed down the crafts concerned with each of these things, and showed [them] magic, and taught astronomy, and the powers of roots, and whatever could never have been found out by human thought; and further the casting of gold and silver and the like, and the varied dyeing of garments. And, in a word, all things that serve the adornment and delight of women are the inventions of the demons bound in flesh.

And from their bastard union bastard men were born, far greater than men in stature, whom afterwards they named giants; not dragon-footed and having waged war against God, as the blasphemous myths of the Greeks sing, but bestial in their ways, and greater than men in size, since they were born of angels, but less than angels, since they had been born of women. So God, knowing that they had grown wild to the point of bestiality, and that the world was not sufficient for their satiety (for it was made in proportion to men and for human use), so that they should not, for their sustenance, turn to the unnatural eating of animals and seem to be blameless, as having dared this out of necessity, the almighty God rained manna on them to suit every desire, and they enjoyed whatever they wished. But they, because of their bastard nature, not content with the purity of the food, craved only the taste of blood. Therefore they were also the first to taste flesh.

Since, then, the souls of the dead giants were greater than human souls, inasmuch as they had also surpassed [them] in their bodies, they were addressed, as a new race, by a new name as well. To these, who were left over in the world, a law was laid down by God through an angel as to how they must live. For being bastards in race, from the fire of angels and the blood of women, and for this reason likely to desire some kind [of thing] of their own, they were forestalled by a just law. For a certain angel was sent to them by God, declaring his will and saying:

This is the decision of the all-seeing God: that you are to lord it over no human being, nor to trouble anyone, unless someone of his own will makes himself your slave, worshipping you, and sacrificing and pouring libations and partaking of your table, or doing anything else that he ought not, or shedding blood, or tasting flesh, or filling himself with what a wild beast has left, or with what has died, or with what is strangled, or with anything else unclean. But those who take refuge in my law you shall not only not touch, but you shall also pay [them] honour, and flee from their presence. For whatever they, being righteous, decide against you, that you will have to suffer. But if any of those who are devoted to me sin, either by committing adultery or by practising magic or by living impurely or by doing anything else that does not please me, then by my command they will have to suffer something from you or from others; and when they repent, I will judge their repentance, whether it is worthy of pardon or not, and give my verdict. These things, then, you are bound to remember, knowing well that not even your thoughts will be able to escape him.

Having given them such commands, the angel departed. But you are still ignorant of this law, that anyone who worships demons, or sacrifices, or shares their table, becomes their slave and will share, as under evil masters, in all the punishment that comes from them; and through this ignorance, having been corrupted at their altars and filled with them, you have come under their power, and you do not know that you are being abused in your bodies in every way. But you ought to know that the demons have power over no one unless someone first becomes their table-companion. For not even their ruler can do anything contrary to the law set in motion by God against them, and for this reason he has no power over anyone who has not worshipped him; but neither can anyone receive from them anything he wants, nor be harmed at all, as [you may] learn.
